speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 104 contains an explanatory note on page 1 which says:
For the convenience and information of members, the orders and regulations of the governor in council specified in the schedule to this act are printed separately and are available to the members in the form of an office consolidation.
About three weeks ago we received this digest or orders in council which is entitled:
An act to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.
Since then I have asked many times, and once again this morning, for a French copy of these regulations and of these orders in council which form part of the bill, and I have been told that there was none. According to section 133 of the British North America Act, which is still in force-
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada . . .
There is no doubt that when we discuss a bill in this house we must have at our disposal both the French and the English versions. Therefore my point is that the second reading of this bill should be postponed as long as the French copy of this consolidation is not printed in French.
To support my contention I would refer Your Honour to standing order 72, which says:
All bills shall be printed before the second reading in the English and French languages.
I refer Your Honour also to page 228 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, paragraph 655, which reads:
When the bill comes up for a second reading in its proper course, one of the clerks at the table will read the order aloud, and the member in charge of the measure will then move its second reading. The member should take care to inform himself whether the bill is printed in the two languages, as that is absolutely necessary at this stage. The letters E.F. on the order paper will show whether that has been done. If any objection be made on that ground, it will prevent the bill being taken up for its second reading on that day.
I refer Your Honour, further, to a decision by the Speaker in 1903, which will be found at page 454 of Beauchesne's, third edition. May I quote what the Speaker said:
I think the question as to the printing of the translation may be taken up only when the bill is being called for its second reading. Should the French translation not be printed at the time of the second reading, then the point of order may be raised.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, my point of order is that this bill should be postponed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I support the point, Mr. Speaker, adding that there is valuable information which I understood the minister was going to make available to the house before second reading. The information asked for was set forth in Hansard. It has to do with a broad category of questions, but I refer in particular to the statement embodying cost of bonuses and subsidies, duties remitted and taxes remitted.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The point of order raised by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) would seem in principle to be well taken, but the hon. member ;s in fact in error. The bill has been printed in the two languages, and the orders in council mentioned in the schedule to the bill have been tabled in both languages. There was distributed for the convenience of hon. members an office consolidation, which has no probative value whatsoever but is a compilation of the orders as they exist now, with the amendments made thereto. That consolidation is not a part of the bill. It is merely a document and one that could not be received in court, that would be no evidence of the orders in council. As I say, it is a convenient document, just as are the other office consolidations of statutes made from time to time.
It was desired to have this convenience- it is merely a matter of convenience-printed in the two languages, but the hon. member probably knows that ever since early in the war the King's Printer has been overburdened with work and has had to let to other printing houses much of the work to be done, and the French translation of this booklet has not yet been received. If it were an official part of the bill the hon, member's point would be well taken, but it is not. It contains, not the orders in the form in which they were tabled, but a compilation of the original orders inserting at the proper places the amendments made by subsequent orders, and it was distributed merely for the convenience of the members so that they might not have to take the originals and themselves put them together to know what was the present form in which an order and its amendments were in force.
The hon. member is perfectly right in saying that everything that is a part of the bill should be in the two languages, and that has been done. The bill has been printed, the schedule has been printed, in the two languages and the orders in council have been tabled in the two languages, but the compilation
Emergency Powers

made for the convenience of members has been received only in the English text and has not yet been received from the King's Printer in the French text. But that is not a necessary document. It is an aid which it might have been convenient to the hon. member to have, but there is no principle involved in the fact that we now seek to proceed without having this additional document in the French language.
I should be quite in accord with my hon. friend if a violation of the principle consecrated by section 133 of the British North America Act were being attempted, but that is not so. The requirements have all been met, and it so happens that the hon. member has not got the two texts of this compilation. But he is fully competent to get the information he wants out of the English version if he wishes to use it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
He did refer to certain requests for information which were made when the measure was in the resolution stage. At the time that information was asked for I said that it would take at least until Monday to get it; thinking, from the circumstances existing at that time, that probably we would still be in committee on Monday. However the bill was reported back on Thursday night; and the next stage is the one we have now reached, namely the motion for second reading. Therefore I propose in the remarks I make this afternoon on second reading to give the main parts of the information asked for on the resolution stage.
I do not know just to what extent it is necessary for me to remind the house of the nature of the measure now before it. I should however point out, I believe, that the orders in council appended to the bill before the house are in no sense new legislation, that these orders in council are now the law of the land, and that they have been the law of the land for years-some of them for many years.
In 1945 this parliament passed the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, which had the effect of extending into and through 1946 powers which theretofore had been exercised under the War Measures Act. At the time the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act was passed there were outstanding a very large number of orders in council- several thousand, in fact. At that time we asked parliament for an extension of powers involving a validation of all these thousands of orders in council, and parliament passed that legislation. It was appropriate legislation for the circumstances of that time. Provision was made for the questioning of any new orders in council that might be passed. Those new orders in council were to be and have been tabled from time to time since.
But when we were preparing the legislation for this year, we felt that we should not ask for an extension of powers to the governor in council, that the time had come when we could rely on the powers already extended to the governor in council by preexisting orders in council, and that if those orders in council were placed before the house, and received its approval, we would not require again any power to legislate for new orders in council. The principle I have just enunciated is the principle of this new legislation.
It is incorrect to call this legislation an extension of emergency power. It is correct to call it a continuation of transitional measures; and that is the reason for the selection of the title of the bill.
Emergency Powers

I believe I should also refer to the fact that this is a greatly contracted list of orders in council, that the overwhelming majority of the orders in council passed during and after ate war are being allowed to lapse. The committee which considered these orders in council from the beginning of 1945 has made an earnest and successful endeavour to keep our wartime order in council legislation-because, in effect, that is what it was, under the War Measures Act-down to very small dimensions, so that the public by picking up the statute, or the readily available documentary material, will know just how much is outstanding. I believe the officials are entitled to congratulations upon the effective and thoroughgoing way in which they have boiled this wartime order in council emergency legislation down to small dimensions.
It may be possible, before the bill is 'through-it is not possible yet-to delete a few orders in council from the schedule. If so *we will move that they be deleted from the schedule. At the present time, however, the need is for the fifty-seven orders in council reference to which is made in the appendix.
It was suggested in the debate on the resolution that we should break into this schedule and take out of it the old age pensions orders in council, the veterans preference orders in council and the labour relations orders in council and now make them the subject of bills. As I understand it, the *reason for the suggestion is that the government has given an undertaking that later in the session it will introduce legislation of what may be described as of a permanent character with respect to these particular matters.
The government has given consideration to this suggestion, and I feel that this is the stage at which I should point out certain relevant facts to the house. Today is the first day of April. If we count today and tomorrow as two days, and if we also count May 15 as a day on which it will be possible for parliament to consider this emergency legislation, parliament will have twenty-six working days to devote to this work. That is the very limit of the time-for both houses. During that time it will be necessary to secure the passage through both houses of the measure now before the house the consideration of which, if it is examined at all carefully, will take many days of the time of both the House of Commons and the other place. In addition there is the other legislation which must be enacted before May 15, unless there is to be a lapse or hiatus. There

by way of address next time. I think it has to be done by act of parliament, which is a considerably more serious matter.
If we took out the three classes of acts to which I have referred and introduced bills and gave them priority over this legislation, I am afraid that we should not be able to complete this legislation by the 15th day of May, in which case we should have again to go through the process of getting an extension if we can, but by act of parliament instead of an address. There need not be much discussion on them, because we shall be ready with our measures as soon as this measure is enacted. The question is whether to have them put on the order paper and perhaps complicate the discussion of this measure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It might shorten it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It might. I will discuss that with the acting leader of the government. It is a suggestion worth considering.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am just placing the problem before the house because I think it has reached the stage where it should be placed before the house and the reasons given why the government is proceeding in this way. [DOT]
As I said in moving the resolution, we are taking what I consider to be a moderate course in asking for an extension of the economic controls, a course not satisfactory by any means to those who believe in the indefinite continuation of controls, and not satisfactory either to those wyho think that controls should be abruptly abandoned. It may have been that in the discussion the other night I tried to summarize the attitude of parties or of groups in parties. I regret it if I did, because I do not see any reason why this should get into politics at all. It is simply a matter of cleaning up, of easing ourselves out of the wartime controls. I know we are accused of having a power complex and of desiring to perpetuate our power, and that the civil servants who are administering these controls are accused of the same thing. There is not much that a person can say by way of disproof of such accusations. We can deny them, which I certainly do. The whole course of our action show's that we are letting go of these powers and getting out of these controls as quickly as it is possible for ans'one to do it. I hope we are not getting out of them too rapidly. I know there are members who think that is the case.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is a whole party feels that way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And we are not ashamed of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would remind the house, as I did the other night, that the government of the dominion cannot maintain these controls indefinitely. It is a matter which undoubtedly reverts to the jurisdiction of the provinces, and we have to get back to that sooner or later. We must continue to adjust ourselves to that inevitable retransfer of the field of jurisdiction from the dominion to the provinces. We have to do it, we ought to do it, and we are doing it. It seems to me that there should not be very much difficulty in the house accepting the principle of this measure on the second reading. I am ready to admit that in the committee stage suggestions may be made for changes here and there in these orders in council. I do not think that they necessarily should be combed with a fine-tooth comb, for this reason, they are so temporary; they are going out. They
Emergency Poxoers

have worked well and there has been no abuse of these orders in council during the past few years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They do all their damage in a short time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Well, my hon. friend and I will not agree on this, but I think they have done immeasurably more good than harm. As I say, I do not think there should be much disagreement in the house about the principle of this measure, but whatever tinkering is done with the provisions of the order in council should be done when we get into committee of the whole.
On the resolution stage a number of questions were asked about the cost of the control policy and also about the benefits of that policy. I have had some inquiries made and I shall try to give that information in a few minutes. Before I do that, however, I want tr, refer to one passage in the speech which I made on the resolution and which can be found at page 1586 of Hansard:	.
The timing of decontrol in the months ahead will be related to economic developments both at home and abroad. Production in Canada and in the United States is now expanding rapidly. In these circumstances, I believe that decontrol is likely to proceed quite rapidly but, as I have emphasized, it is the government's intention to avoid disorderly price fluctuations and confused markets which abrupt abandonment of all controls would be certain to produce.
That sums up I think as best I can the policy of the government with reference to decontrol, the avoidance of abrupt abandonment of all controls and of the disorderly price fluctuations and confused markets which this abrupt abandonment will be certain to produce, while proceeding with decontrol as rapidly as possible under all the circumstances.
Later this afternoon my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will announce a further measure of decontrol. It will not go as far as those who are opposed to controls are urging, and it will certainly go too far to please those who think there should not be any lifting of price ceilings at all. It is based upon the principles to be found in the quotation I have just read. It will free from price ceilings a further list of commodities which the government and the board feel can safely be fixed at this time. But-and I should like to emphasize this-the volume of goods still under price ceilings will be important, far-reaching and substantial. It will still include a large proportion of the essential requirements of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minister has gone this far; will he now tell us what articles the
[Mr. Ilsley.)
controls are to be lifted from? He has whetted our curiosity and caused us some misgiving as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance will make a statement later this afternoon.
With regard to the request for the total cost or the average cost per year of the stabilization policy, I was asked to make a compilation of wartime prices and trade board subsidies and trading losses, the cost of administration of the wartime prices and trade board, the Department of Agriculture subsidies, other subsidies, such as wheat and flour subsidies, the amount of the remission in duties and taxes and other subsidies such as the coal subsidies paid by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply; that is, the subsidies, the tax and duty remissions, and the costs of administration connected with our stabilization policy. I said I doubted whether I should be able to obtain an accurate computation of the tax and duty remissions. As a matter of fact that is so. These removals or remissions of duties and taxes fall into three broad categories: first, removal or reduction of intermediate and general rates of duty where normal preferential sources of supply were cut off by war or surrendered by Canada in the interests of economy in shipping. These are a number of examples: anthracite coal in the maritime provinces where United States supplies had to replace British supplies; crude rubber-Malaya being cut off, we had to rely on United States stocks and South American production; tin-Malaya being cut off we had to draw on United States stocks and South American production; copra and palm kernels -Belgian colonial supplies replaced in part British colonial supplies; sugar-the removal of full duties because we gave up more distant empire sources, for example, Australia, South America, Mauritius and even part of the British West Indies, and drew supplies from Cuba and Santo Domingo; oranges- seasonal duty which conferred a preference on empire sources was removed, since these were unavailable; rice-with the loss of Burma we had to take United States supplies; combed wool-we had to rely more heavily on United States combing mills because United Kingdom facilities were not available.
I should like to point out that with regard to that type of importation it would be completely unfair to add up the remissions of the general rate of duty and say that that was part of the cost of the stabilization policy, because very little was imported from these sources before the war. They were imported from British preference countries where the rate of duty was very much lower. For

Emergency Powers
instance, we switched to some extent in our importations of sugar from British preferential sources to Cuba and Santo Domingo where the rate of duty was $1.29 instead of 29 cents, but we did not pay the $1.29. That was taken off. Therefore it would be unfair to reckon the cost to the country of that policy by taking $1.29, because the situation was entirely abnormal. It had not been paid before the war, and probably it will not be paid after the war. It was just a new situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Before the minister leaves sugar, will he say something about the excise tax on refined sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With regard to refined sugar the situation before the war was that there was a tax of one cent a pound on refined sugar, or $1 on 100 pounds. We raised that to two cents in 1941, and then we took half the increase off in 1942 and the other half of it off in 1943, 'bringing our tax on sugar back to exactly what it was before the war. The excise tax is the same as it was before the war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Was there not an excise tax on sugar before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was one cent, and it is the same now. One cent has been taken off, half at one time and half at another. My hon. friend had really no point there. The point that he had was on the British preferential rates of duty on sugar which were remitted. He had a point there. That was part of the cost of our stabilization policy, and I am told that it amounted to about two and a half millions a year, but not these big sums.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister allow me-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Just a minute. I am making a speech on the second reading and I am sorry I have to deal with this mass of facts at this stage, but I am obliged to because my hon. friends wanted it at an early stage. The second class of duty and tax removal was of special wartime taxes imposed at an early stage in the war and removed at a later stage, examples of which would be the extra or additional tax of one cent per pound on sugar imposed in April 1941 and removed in two stages in 1942 and 1943, and-to take another example-the special taxes on tea and coffee imposed in September 1939 and removed in 1942.
Is that part of the cost of stabilization policy? I do not think so. They were not traditional, long-standing taxes at all but were put on and taken off again, and I do not think they should be reckoned in it. Where the 83166-123
removal or reduction of the tax was primarily to protect the stabilization policy, this wa3 part of cost. Examples would include the remission of the preferential duty on sugar and the suspension of the duty on bananas and of the seasonal duties on certain fresh fruits and vegetables.
It would be impossible to calculate exactly the theoretical loss of revenue by reason of these removals or remissions of duties and taxes. Had these duties remained on and the prices of the commodities been increased by the amount of the duty, the quantity imported might have declined, that is to say, less of these commodities might have been purchased. But even if this very real difficulty be ignored, it would take a great deal of time to compile the kind of table which the hon. member requested. In some cases the duty was suspended for only a short period of weeks, at a time of seasonal shortage in Canada-for example, on onions in the spring of 1944 and on new potatoes for a few weeks in 1945. In other cases the duty was suspended only for a particular use, for example, coke when used for cooking or heating. In still other cases the duty was suspended in the middle of a month and reimposed in the middle of another month, and it would be almost impossible to ascertain the quantities imported free of duty in broken months.
I cite these points as an explanation of why I cannot give my hon. friend the exact detail for which he has asked. Even to prepare as full and accurate a statement as might be possible would take a great deal of time and labour. I am advised, however, that a quick check of the list of tax removals or suspensions indicates that the amount of revenue forgone would be of the order of $5 million or $6 million in the full year, excluding remissions of duty on account of changed sources of supply dictated by war conditions, and excluding the removal of taxes imposed at an earlier stage in the war. The true figure might be a little below or a little above this. I cannot be exact without having a great deal of statistical work done on this question.
But let me come to the larger question of the total cost of this policy. The following figures give a rough approximation of the annual averages for the five years from 1942 to 1946 inclusive: wartime prices and trade board administration, $12 million; wartime prices and trade board subsidies and trading losses, $84 million.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yearly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes. This is the average of five years. Department of Agriculture subsidies, $65 million. I am not at all sure that

Emergency Powers

they should all be charged to the stabilization policy, because I believe some of them were quality subsidies to encourage production of higher quality. To continue: Wheat and flour subsidies paid by the Department of Finance, $15 million.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mainly to bakers and millers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Millers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes; that is what I meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That was paid to millers for the purpose of keeping the price of flour and bread down, the subsidies being repaid in part when the profit position justified it. Next, remission of duties, et cetera, $5 million. That is a rough, a very rough estimate. Then there were coal subsidies paid by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply amounting to $5 million. The total is $186 million per annum on the average.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) put a question and pressed me to answer it, and I will do this as best, I can, although it is almost impossible to give an answer to the question. He asked for an estimate of the benefits to the citizens of Canada as a result of the price control policies; that is to say, the saving in prices to the consumer-the amount by which consumer prices were made lower than they otherwise would have been.
The following estimate gives some indication of the strain and difficulty which would have developed in the Canadian economy without price control. It is based on the assumption that in the absence of price control prices would hare risen in recent years to the same extent that they rose in world war I and its aftermath. Nobody knows whether they would or would not, or would have risen higher.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is an impractical question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I wish to point out that we never devoted more than 15 per cent of our resources to the war in any year of world war I, whereas in world war II, in some years, we devoted approximately fifty per cent of the production of the country to the war. And economists have always told me that that is the main factor in driving prices up-the proportion of output that you shoot away and send away, leaving in the country the purchasing power that was paid out to produce it, and nothing to spend it on. That is a powerful inflationary influence. It must be remembered that in many countries where there existed no effective control, prices were going up 100,
[Mr. Ilsley-i
200 and 300 per cent, and I am not talking of wild inflations such as occurred in China and other places. But if we assume that prices would have risen, and the inflationary factors were more powerful in the last few years than in the years between 1914 and 1920, much more powerful,-if we assume. I say, that prices would have risen, without control, just to the same extent proportionally, year by year, as they did in the period from 1914 to 1919. then these are the results you get: the consumers would have had to spend an average of nearly $8 billion between 1942 and 1946.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How many millions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I said, nearly $8 billion a year between 1942 and 1946, to buy goods and services, which in fact cost them on the average not quite $6-5 billion a year. If hon. gentlemen want to know how that is arrived at they can procure table 11, gross national expenditure at market prices, 1938 to 1946, issued by the bureau of statistics, which shows the personal expenditure on consumer goods and services for each of the years from 1938 to 1946; and if the amount spent had increased proportionately [DOT] to the increase in prices in the first great war, the amount spent would have averaged $8 billion in those years instead of the $62 billion which the consumers actually did spend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does that take into consideration the higher taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No; it does not take that into account. Taxation was part of the stabilization policy. High income taxes were probably the most powerful factor in the anti-inflation policy. In short, if prices had risen as they did in the last war and its aftermath, the consumers would have had to spend $14 billion more than they actually did.
It should also be noted that the general stabilization programme held down the cost of munitions and other military expenses, thereby saving a further large addition to the already heavy national debt. It is estimated that government expenditures averaged $4 billion a year between 1942 and 1946. Without price control this cost might have been at the very least twenty-five per cent higher. I think that twenty-five per cent is based upon the other figures which I have given with regard to the additional percentage which the consumers would have been obliged to pay; and the stabilization programme has thus meant a saving of another billion dollars a year. From these estimates it is possible to see that the cost of the control programme was under $200 million a year, while the savings to the con-

Emergency Powers
sumer purchasers and government as a buyer were on this hypothesis possibly $2 i billion a year. The figures are tentative but do give some idea of the relative magnitude of the cost of and the savings effected by the government price control programme.
The validity of the cost of living index figures was questioned. I cannot go into the basis of the cost of living index. It has been thoroughly debated in previous sessions and exhaustive material has been placed before the house. The trouble is that the materia! is so exhaustive that it does not make popular reading. It takes a good deal of work to go through it. But the bureau of statistics assert and appear to be able to establish that their cost of living index is a very reliable one, and that there is no better cost of living index in any country.

But the minister will
admit that it does not put milk into the mouths of babies, and that it does not put into the homes other things which the housewives need.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext: I will ask the question, if it has to be a question, although it is difficult to frame it.

speechtext: All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As I say, the cost of living index is, I think, a good index. Somebody said that articles no longer being produced are in the index. That statement is flatly denied. They are not left in there at all if they are not available in Canada.
I hesitate to get into this question of the validity of the comparison of the price rise in Canada and the United States. I have a good 83166-1231
deal of material on it, but it is detailed, and it is mainly estimates. The points were made by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), mainly. He said that we had paid subsidies and that the Americans had taken, their subsidies off during the period, that we continued to pay them. The weakness in that is that the Americans had taken most of their subsidies off before the period began. They had only two subsidies that we can find out about, the meat subsidy and the flour subsidy. The other answer to the argument is that most of our rise in the cost of living during that period has been due to the removal of our subsidies; so there does not seem to be much of any point left.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) does not perhaps understand what I am saying, but if we had a situation like this, where we had at the beginning of the period full subsidies on in the United States and full subsidies on in Canada on a comparable basis and then six months later the United States subsidies had gone off and the Canadian subsidies had stayed on, the taking off of the United States subsidies would obviously be the cause of several points rise in the United States index; and there would not have been a comparable factor in Canada. But the situation was altogether different from that. Most of the United States subsidies were taken off before that period began; many of the Canadian subsidies were taken off during the period, and most of our price rise was due to the fact, that we took those subsidies off.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question while we are on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I see the point the minister has made, but I still ask him this question. When we have been using comparative figures between such and such a rise in the United States and such and such a rise here, which was an over-all figure, and when we have been using, as I understand, during the same period, which was from the middle of 1945 to the middle of 1946. figures which did not include subsidies, does the minister not agree that in order to get a comparison during these periods it is necessary to carry in, if he can carry in, the proper figure of our subsidies which were being paid by the taxpayers of Canada to assist in keeping down that price? In other words, does he not agree that these figures, unless we carry in our subsidy payments, are not comparable?
Emergency Powers

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not talking about comparative prices, and I did not think hon. gentlemen opposite were talking about comparative prices. They were talking about comparative increases, and they were saying that the comparison between the increases was an unfair comparison because we have maintained our subsidies and the Americans have taken off theirs. Now what I am saying is that they took off most of their subsidies before the period began, and our subsidies have been coming off since, so the validity of the comparison holds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is always possible that I may not have understood the minister, but let me come back at the point. One of these figures given is the figure of the rise over the period of 1935 to 1939-in other words, just before the war-until, I think, the end of 1945 or 1946. Surely the minister will agree that in order to make a comparison between what happened in the United States and what happened in Canada we must take in the Canadian subsidies in order to show what the actual cost of living in Canada was. After all, these United States comparisons are relied on, I think, as the strongest argument of any in pointing to the success of our own control of costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Our comparisons have been in the increases. We have said that when the Americans decontrolled in the middle of last year, their cost of living shot up by about eighteen points in six months and ours stayed down to four or five, or something like that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Six.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Six, during that same period. We are not talking about price. Price is a different thing entirely. That is another argument; I cannot get into that question of the comparison of the price levels in the two countries. We are talking about the validity of the comparison of increases, and the government is virtually accused of putting up something here which is very misleading, because the Americans have taken off their subsidies. The removal of hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies would, of course, put up their prices, and if we kept our subsidies on that would indicate it was purely the subsidies which were doing the work, or very nearly that. But we have quite a different situation. When they had their subsidies off very largely at the beginning of the period, it could not have been the removal of the .subsidies which put up their prices; and when
I Mr. Maedonnell.]
we were taking off our subsidies during the period it was largely the removal of the subsidies here that put our prices up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not want to press the point, but on the other hand, since the minister has brought me into it-I did not do it myself-I think I should say that I still believe the minister has overlooked one point. These comparisons, which are constantly made, are made as a result of what is alleged or taken to be the figure given as to the cost of living in Canada. I still maintain that when that cost is given without including the subsidies it is not a complete figure, and that when used as a comparative figure it gives an unsound picture. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend is now arguing that when you compile a cost of living index that should not be done by putting into it only the cost of the articles the families of Canada buy, that is the cost to those families, but that some tax feature should be carried into it as well, some income tax. or something like that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes; a subsidy which is used to pay part of the cost. I do argue that, definitely.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But I suggest-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just a moment, now. I am making a speech on second reading, or was a short time ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Very well. You brought me into it and now I shall get out.	. .	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
After all, we are not in committee yet. The other point was the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. Any change in an exchange rate will, of course, affect the cost of imports. Again it is not possible to be precise, but I am advised that the direct effect on the Canadian index of the return to parity with the United States dollar would have been about one-half of one per cent. Return to parity of course reduced our subsidy costs considerably, and by reducing the cost of certain imported raw materials and industrial fuels it eased some of the upward pressure on production costs in Canada. After all, Mr. Speaker, I am answering points here directed mostly to the validity of certain arguments we have put forward on behalf of price control, and I do

Emergency Powers
not think we should get too far away from the principle of the bill and the simple question as to whether or not these economic controls should be allowed to lapse. That is the simple question: should they be allowed to lapse or not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the minister going to say why we revaluated the Canadian dollar, or is that too big a question to answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No. I dealt with that last summer, when I made a statement on the matter, and I do not want to go into it again. I have not very much more to say this afternoon because so much has been said at previous stages.
Perhaps I should say something about the constitutional basis of the bill. This bill is based upon the existence of a national emergency arising out of the war. One of the clauses in the preamble reads:
And whereas the national emergency arising out of the war, in certain aspects, has continued since the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan and is still continuing . . .
The emergency in its military aspects has, in the opinion of some, largely disappeared, but in its economic aspects has continued since the termination of hostilities and still continues, for the reasons and in the way set out in the speech I made in this house when I introduced the resolution.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I might ask the minister one question before he concludes, and I think it is on the principle of the bill. He has just said, as I understood him, that this is an emergency matter largely having to do with prices. In view of the fact that labour matters automatically go back to the provinces; in view of the further fact that all ceilings have been removed from salaries and wages, can the minister tell me where there is any emergency in connection with that matter? I can see the emergency argument elsewhere, but I am utterly unable to see it with respect to the dominion government maintaining its position in reference to labour matters. Perhaps the minister would answer that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton) r Mr. Speaker, it is clear now that the appeals made to the government and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) during the resolution-stage for a different procedure, which would offer the house an opportunity to approach this question in an orderly way and which would save time, have been rejected. By reason of the course chosen by the government the house is now left to flounder in what can only be called a legislative morass.
This is a measure of the highest importance. I do not suppose any legislation to come before the house this session will equal in importance the measure now occupying our attention; and the stage we have reached now is, I submit, of prime importance. At the resolution stage we were invited by the Minister of Justice to defer discussion until after the introduction of the bill. That invitation was accepted and endorsed by my leader. Others did not follow it, however, and discussion took place. Now
Emergency Powers

the Minister of Justice is proposing that the house defer intensive consideration of the measure in its leading aspects until second reading is given andi the house is in committee. We have had a number of requests, always to defer consideration, and I think the reason is quite obvious. The government invites the house to pass over those aspects of the consideration that the house ought to give this bill which are likely to give them the greatest difficulty. In view of the fact that we are now at the stage of second reading, and that it is necessary at this stage to deal with the principle of the bill, I ask the house now to endeavour, by examination of the provisions of the bill, to find the principle of it, if there be a principle in it.
I am not going to discuss the terms of the measure in detail. But I wish to refer to enough of the contents of the bill to try, if it be possible, to find the principle of it. As the Minister of Justice has indicated, the preamble purports to base the bill upon the continuing existence of a national emergency arising out of the war. Hon. members will find that language repeated in the preamble. And they will find a qualification, in one of the references, in the expression "in certain aspects". Finally it is said that the bill is put forward in order to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace.
What follows? We have, first of all, the -provision that certain orders and regulations, referred to in the schedule to the bill-and referred to by number, name and date only- are to be continued. They are to continue and be in force while the act is in force.
Then we have the provision that the governor in council may appoint such persons in connection with the administration of any order or regulation continued in force by the act as he considers necessary, and may fix their compensation. It is further provided that all persons who have been appointed under the War Measures Act or the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act in connection with the administration of any of these orders or regulations are deemed to have been appointed pursuant to the provisions of the act. Parliament will never have any part in making such appointments, but automatically they are deemed to have been appointed pursuant to the provisions of the act.
It provides further that the governor in council may revoke in whole or in part any order or regulation continued in force by or made under this act. The operation of the act is to be limited so as not to extend
[iMr. Fleming.]
beyond March 31, 1948, but it may be extended by resolution passed by both houses of parliament.
It is further provided that all orders and regulations continued in force under the authority of the act shall be deemed to be regulations, under the provisions of the Interpretation Act.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the bill. Attached to it is a schedule containing references-and only references-to some fifty-seven orders in council, orders in council under which vast numbers of other orders have, in turn, been made. Where is the principle of the bill? I submit to the house that, so far as a solemn legislative act on the part of the house is concerned, the full knowledge and appreciation of what is involved in the step parliament is asked to take is lacking. There is. in that sense, no principle in the bill.
The only principle that can be found in it, in the manner in which it has been presented to the house, is this, that a government which has grown accustomed during time of war to treat parliament with something between tolerance and contempt, has decided that it will ask parliament to give legislative sanction, willy-nilly and holus-bolus, to a whole volume of legislation, in a manner which absolutely precludes any detailed examination by parliament of the language of the orders to which it is proposed that statutory effect shall be given.
We are asked to swallow the measure on second reading-and in one swallow.
We are not given an opportunity of looking at certain of these measures and saying, "Some are of a temporary nature, while some in their subject matter obviously relate to subjects requiring permanent legislation." Parliament is not permitted to say, "We approve some of these measures; we disapprove others." No, we are asked on second reading to accept the bill and, in effect, to give blanket endorsement to a measure which, I say, is lacking in any principle upon which parliament can pass intelligently. To isolate the principle of the bill so that parliament may apply its intelligence to that principle is impossible under the circumstances created by the government. Parliament has been invited to stultify itself.
The method followed by the government is such as to thwart any attempt on the part of parliament to do its duty, to examine in every letter and detail the legislation it is asked to enact. The explanation is, of course, that our appeals to reason have fallen on deaf ears. Rigidity, again, has triumphed in the government.

Emergency Powers
The Minister of Justice has made reference to the situation which confronted the government and parliament at the outset of this session. He referred to the fact that the powers conferred upon the governor in council by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act would come to an end on March 29, and that therefore the government found it necessary to secure from parliament specific legislative sanction for orders in council it deemed to be essential, or to ask for a general extension of the power to make such orders.
He has professed a desire for decontrol. Other members of the administration have professed a desire for decontrol. Most confusing statements have come from the government benches on this subject of its attitude toward decontrol. Sometimes there have been expressions in terms of advocacy of decontrol, and at other times there have been held up to parliament threats of national chaos if any further measures of decontrol were proposed. In this, parliament has not enjoyed clear leadership from the government; it has had only confusion thrown in its way.
At the outset of the session there were suggestions from the government-as a matter of fact one finds reference to this in the speech from the throne

to a desire on the part of the government to depart from the method of legislation by orders in council. It will be recalled that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, paused for one fleeting moment to do an act of devotion at the shrine of the supremacy of parliament. But we have been looking in vain for some indication on the part of the government that it really means seriously to restore to parliament the full supremacy of parliament which it lost in time of war at the hands of this administration, and which must be returned to it, now that we are in a time of peace.
The Minister of Justice did not repeat today the expressions he used on March 20. when introducing the legislation. I should like to remind the house of the test which the minister proposed to apply to all measures affected by the present bill. At page 1583 of Hansard he is reported in these words:
Only the extreme nature of the emergency with which the country was faced justified the vesting of such powers in the executive.
And, Mr. Speaker, only measures passing that test-and it must be a severe and acid test-can, in my submission, be considered by parliament as worthy of continuance now- nearly two years after the conclusion of the war-under the guise of a continuing national emergency.
What did the government do? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to recall the course which the government itself followed at the outset of this session. It introduced from time to time into the house no less than fifteen specific bills, bills in each case arising out of the fact that the orders in council which owed their validity to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act would be coming to an end on March 29. Every one of these fifteen measures arose out of the termination of these orders in council. Some of these measures are of a permanent nature; some of them have time limits contained within their terms. Here they are, and I ask you, sir, and I ask the house to consider them in comparison with many of the orders m council to which reference is made in the schedule to the bill now before the house: the Immigration Act amendment, containing provisions permanent in their nature; Export and Import Permits Act, a measure which is given the life of one year; the Canada Grain Act amendment; Militia Pension Act amendment; Customs Act amendment; Foodstuffs Act amendment; Inspection and Sale Act amendment; Fertilizers Act amendment; Militia Act amendment; Patent Act amendment; Supplemental Payments on Mail Contracts Act; Department of National Defence Act; Trading with the Enemy Act; Wheat Board Act amendment; Agricultural Products Act. All these are permanent in their effect, with two possible exceptions. Most of them are amendments to statutes of parliament. Two of them are of a limited duration as appears by their terms. One to which I have referred, the Export and Import Permits Act, is given by its own terms the life of one year, and the Trading with the Enemy Act seems, if one can make anything of the language of that bill, to be intended to have a limited duration. You will have seen, Mr. Speaker, that most of these measures are in the form of permanent legislation. In the light of that fact and the fact that the government has already introduced measures of a permanent nature in at least thirteen bills and two others of perhaps a semi-permanent or interim nature, I ask why it was that when the government came to measures of the kind we find in the schedule to this bill it stopped short and did not proceed to introduce bills of a permanent nature which it indicates it intends to introduce at a later stage of the present session. It just does not make sense.
There is no distinction in principle between measures of the kind that the government has already introduced and a number of the orders in council in the schedule to this bill. Instead, the government has seen fit to present to this house in their full variety fifty-seven .measures
Emergency Powers

rolled into one, in my submission the greatest hodge-podge of legislation ever presented to this house. I ask the house-this is not new- to have regard to the variety of subject matter contained in the measures referred to in the schedule to this bill. Think of it! Rolled into one measure we have this infinite variety, this hodge-podge of subject matter: Recovery of subsidies on food and the- payment of such subsidies; preference in the civil service for ex-service men; exemption of imported anthracite coal from customs duty; exemption of coke made from coal from the war exchange tax when used for certain purposes; exemption of bagging material from customs duty when imported; tariff provisions with reference to well-drilling machinery; the. whole broad scope of the powers and jurisdiction of the wartime prices and trade board, the most powerful body ever established by any government in Canada; the whole group of orders dealing with rent controls in Canada; those dealing with the incorporation and powers of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation and the regulations made by it; the repayment of subsidies under the authority of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation; the banking of ration coupons; the Government Employees Compensation Act-another act already introduced at this session; the consolidation of supplementary regulations; the order dealing with -the power and jurisdiction of the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation ; regulations for the control of salt fishing; pelagic sealing regulations; the canned fish allocation regulations; prohibition of fishing licences to persons of the Japanese race; the authorization of appeals in. cases involving breaches of the wartime regulations; wartime labour relations regulations, involving the whole scope of collective bargaining, and the procedure consequent upon it; the protection of certifications granted under the Ontario collective bargaining act and the establishment of wartime labour relations boards in certain of the provinces; financial assistance to voluntary repatriates to Japan of persons of the Japanese race; the reservation to the crown of radioactive substances in the Yukon territory; the reservation to the crown of similar substances in the northwest territories; postdischarge benefits to the members of the armed services serving in the interim forces; regulations relating to naval, military and air force estates; regulations involving claims by or against the crown involving members of the armed forces serving overseas; salvage services by His Majesty's Canadian ships; payment of old age pensions and pensions for the blind; the regulation of the distribution of construction materials; emergency shelter 
regulations-sweeping powers conferred first on the minister and now on the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; orders dealing with wartime industries control, steel control, timber control; administration by the custodian of enemy property of property of persons of the Japanese race; transfer to the custodian of the property of Japanese evacuees; compensation to seamen for damage to their effects; authorization to the chairman of the board of steamship inspection to relieve ships from certain provisions of the Canada Shipping Act; a measure dealing with permission to Canadian chartered ships to clear on a voyage with masters, mates or engineers not holding appropriate certificates; and, finally, regulations dealing with an allowance to merchant seamen, who are out of work.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that if you take down every volume of legislation enacted by parliament and scan the subject matter embraced within the enactments in any one session you will look in vain for any volume containing such a tremendous variety of subject matter as you find in this one measure that is before the house today. There has not yet been on the part of the government any attempt to assist the house by breaking down this legislation and taking out of it, in the first place, the measures which the government frankly admits to be legislative in their nature. We made a plea for a breakdown because it would assist orderly procedure and save the time of the house, but the government has not seen fit to do that.
The Minister of Justice said that the orders were of three kinds, regulative, administrative and legislative. Of the legislative we have some requiring permanent legislation. In the first place, we have the orders dealing with old age pensions. By the government's own statement they are to be replaced by legislation this session. We have those dealing with labour relations and with the civil service preference.

The orders that I have enumerated in these three categories number ten; but there are still other orders the need for which will come to an end as soon as the new legislation has been adopted. I refer particularly to six orders under the heading of the Department of Labour, which are attached to the bill. There are at least sixteen which, in my submission, are quite unnecessary and illogical to have included within the scope of the bill. The others could be regrouped in a way which would assist the house greatly, for example, those of a permanent nature such as the two dealing with radioactive substances in the territories, and those which are of a strictly temporary nature. Hon. members wish to be sure that there is no hiatus in the matter of these orders relating to old age pensions and pensions for the blind. I am sure that there would be strong support throughout the house for the continuation of rent control regulations, not necessarily in the precise form in which they appear today, but in general, and particularly in urban centres. But we are asked today to vote on second reading of the bill, without any opportunity to say which of these measures in this great vast volume we are prepared to support and which we are not.
The procedure which the government is following cannot fail to make it impossible for a clear expression of opinion to be given on the measure at this time. The Minister of Justice touched on the point that the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act will expire on May 15. Hon. members have told him, and I am sure it would be a matter of general consent, that as to these orders which ought to be the subject of permanent legislation there will be no objection, if the house has not had all the time necessary by May 15 to complete its detailed review of these measures, to permitting these particular orders to be continued for any necessary period. But the method followed by the government, without regard to the fact that, since it has proposed to introduce this measure, there has been an extension of time to May 15, precludes parliament from giving effective expression of opinion on the second reading of the bill.
I wish to speak briefly on the subject of emergency. The Minister of Justice said today that he supports the bill on the ground of emergency. The resolution which the house passed gave the government leave to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war. Yet the government in almost the same breath tells us that a number of these orders are to be replaced by permanent legislation covering the same subject matter and having no relation whatever to the national emergency referred to in the resolution or in the preamble to the bill. We are being asked to legislate in this respect what is nothing but a fiction. If the Minister of Justice proposes to ask this house to support the continuance of orders which are to be replaced later this session by permanent legislation, on the ground that they must be continued because of a national emergency, if there is any emergency with reference to these orders it is not attributable to the war; it is attributable to the policy of the government in not bringing down legislation at the proper time, which is early in the session.
The house has not been assisted by what the Minister of Justice has had to say on the subject of the constitutional position of parliament in purporting to legislate under emergency powers. What the Minister, of Justice has done is only to succeed in adding to the confusion in the house by the maimer in which the bill has been presented. I again recall the opinion of the law officers of the crown submitted by the Minister of Justice to the house on this very point on March 20, which may be found at page 1553 of Hansard. Perhaps that is the Minister of Justice's idea of trying to save the time of the house. He can have it either way. It will be found at page 1716 of Hansard of March 25 in the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). He is quoting from the speech of the 
Minister of Justice to which I have referred. Here we have the quotation from the statement made by the Minister of Justice on March 20:
Our emergency legislation is based on the existence of a national emergency arising out of the war, on the emergency doctrine . . .
And further on:
However I shall add my own opinion. I think on most occasions it will be the same as that of the deputy minister.
Again referring, Mr. Speaker, to the opinion of the deputy minister of justice that it is no longer necessary to rely strictly on the doctrine of emergency, that the effect of the recent decisions of the privy council has been to extend the power of parliament, so that parliament in these cases is not held down strictly to the four corners of the emergency principle as interpreted in the Fort Frances case of earlier days. And here we have a further quotation:
I am not going to venture into an opinion on the matter.
These, again, are the words of the Minister of Justice:
I am not going to venture into an opinion on the matter. However I have read the Canada Temperance Act case and the subsequent case, that of the Japanese reference, and it appears to me that the true effect of the decision in the Canada Temperance Act case is that there does not have to be an emergency to found jurisdiction on the part of the dominion; that the dominion may have the power even when there is no emergency to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, even though its legislation touches upon matters ordinarily regarded as solely within provincial jurisdiction. In other words, the judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council as given by Lord Simon extends rather than narrows the powers of the dominion as they had heretofore been conceived.
Again we find these words from the statement of the Minister of Justice:
As I say, these cannot be the only aspects of the emergency but these aspects are, I submit, sufficient to occasion a valid exercise of the powers under the peace, order and good government clause.
To sum up: We do not need, under the Canada Temperance Act case, to establish a national emergency.
Could anything be more thoroughly calculated to confuse this house in its endeavour to measure the extent of any national emergency which is alleged to exist in certain aspects, necessitating some fifty-seven orders in council? The fact of the matter is that the insertion by the government of these words "in some aspects" in relation to the alleged national emergency shows conclusively that it is incumbent upon the government to establish,

Emergency Powers
with reference to each of these orders, with reference to each subject matter dealt with within the broad scope of the fifty-seven orders, the existence of a national emergency in that particular aspect, the aspect relating to the subject matter of each of these orders in council. And that cannot be done. It is an impossibility to do it on the second reading. In the light of the confusing statements made by the Minister of Justice on this subject of jurisdiction, how can it be expected that parliament, with this hodge-podge thrown at it by the government, can give a proper and intelligent expression of opinion on the alleged principle of this bill?
Then, Mr. Speaker, I offer this observation just in passing from the subject of emergency. It is, of course, the habit of the government to refer to the emergency that existed during the time of war, and the function that was fulfilled in time of war by certain of these controls. We could admit all that sort of thing, and it would not advance us one iota towards an orderly consideration of the problem presented by the bill.
We are not now considering what happened during the time of war, when this country faced a grave crisis, the greatest in its history, along with the forces of freedom throughout the rest of the world. What we are dealing with today, nearly two years after the conclusion of hostilities, is the situation we find ourselves in at the present time, a situation in which the government must, in my submission, prove with respect to each of these fifty-seven measures the existence of a national emergency with relation to that particular subject. There must be proofs on these fifty-seven aspects if the government is to have a sound constitutional foundation for legislation of this kind, and that goes to the root of the whole question. It establishes, it seems to me, the utter impossibility of the government justifying the principle of a bill like this when the constitutionality of the measure can be established only by reference to each of the fifty-seven orders and proving that, for the special subject matter of each order individually, there exists a national emergency.
We had hoped, during the consideration in committee of the whole, at any rate, on the resolution, to have received from the government some clear statement of its objective with reference to decontrol. I am afraid we have just about as clear an idea now of the government's objective as we had when we started.

I come now to the terms of the bill and the important schedule to it, Mr. Speaker. In the first place, I submit to you that the bill is quite improper in its composition or in the form that it takes as submitted to this house. What we have is simply reference to a number of these measures by order, by subject and by date. The Minister of Justice makes a big play of his claim that when the house resolves itself into committee of the whole an opportunity will be provided for all members to scrutinize these orders and to amend them. Let us have some regard to the facts. What have we in the bill before us? Suppose, when we come to the order dealing with rent control, I wish to make an amendment to the order to provide that veterans who have purchased houses in good

Emergency Powers
faith for their personal occupancy should not be denied occupation of them; how am I to do that? Apparently, I must, in committee of the whole, make reference to an order which is some pages in length, and somehow try to put before the house some particular provision. I do not know how I am to refer to it unless I say page number so-and-so, line number so-and-so in this volume which we are told is not before the house. We were told as much this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). How on earth is the house, in committee of the whole, to apply its intelligence to deal with these measures individually, seriatim, and pass upon them line by line and page by page? The method followed by the government will just defy any effort to bring order out of chaos, even in committee of the whole. An insuperable problem has been created in the procedure which has been adopted.
I wish to make this further observation in conclusion. I suppose it is not to be wondered at that many of us in this house approach with a measure of suspicion a proposal from the government that vast, sweeping powers be conferred on bodies outside the house, when we have regard to the fact that, over the period of years during which some of these orders have been in effect, we saw the eclipse of parliament while the strength of the controllers grew; when we saw orders in council being passed even while parliament was in session; when we saw necessary information denied to parliament on the ground that it was not in the public interest; when secret orders were made and information concerning them was denied to this house. And when today we see no objective toward which decontrol could move on an orderly basis; when we see rather on every hand the continuation of the bureaucratic complex; when we see an attempt made on the government side-and joined in, of course, by their allies, the socialists-to perpetuate this centralization of power at Ottawa into the time of peace, small wonder it is, in the light of all these facts, that we approach a measure of this kind with a certain degree of suspicion.
We do not look for a too frank interpretation on the part of some parties of the stand we are taking on this measure. We are taking a stand to this effect. In the light of the way in which the government have presented this measure, the way in which they have created confusion by the procedure which they have followed, the way in which they have prevented parliament from trying to bring any order out of the chaos of government creation, we say that there is no principle which can be isolated
from this bill and on which parliament can be asked to pass an intelligent opinion. And we say that, until there is clear justification, we do not wish to put parliament in the position of simply abdicating great powers in favour of bureaucratic boards outside parliament. Let it not be said that we are opposing these orders in council holus-bolus, because that cannot be said honestly by anyone. What we say is that, on a measure framed in the terms in which this one is framed, and following the procedure on this bill which the government insists should be followed in the face of appeals to reason, it is impossible for this house to pass on the principle of this bill; and that is not to be taken as opposition to all these orders in council, because we simply say that we are not prepared to swallow everything holus-bolus. Whatever is good and whatever is bad have been mixed together here in such a way that it is impossible to extricate the one from the other.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in order that the position taken by the official opposition may be clearly before the house and before the people, and in order that the position we take may not be open to misinterpretation by political adversaries, let me now present to the house an amendment which I offer, seconded by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling):
That all the words after "that" he deleted and the following substituted therefor:

This house is unalterably opposed to the enactment of a measure to continue indiscriminately the sweeping powers of the presently existing boards outside the control of parliament."
